modules.title: Core Python
modules.intro: Core Python interview questions are the baseline for every Python backend role. This page covers the language fundamentals that interviewers probe regardless of framework — the four built-in data structures (list, dict, set, tuple), string immutability and interning, exception handling with all four clauses (try/except/else/finally), Python's data model, and the small comparisons that come up in every screen (list vs tuple, == vs is, mutable vs immutable). For OOP-heavy questions (dunder methods, metaclasses, SOLID in Python) head to the dedicated Python OOP page. Each answer is structured the way you'd actually deliver it in a 45-minute interview: the headline, the why, a short code shape, and the trade-off the interviewer is really listening for.

modules.title: Python OOP & SOLID
modules.intro: Python OOP interview questions go beyond syntax — interviewers want to know whether you think in objects or just write classes. This page covers the four OOP pillars as Python expresses them (duck typing, mixins, @property, __slots__), the dunder protocol (__init__, __repr__, __eq__, __hash__, __enter__, __exit__), metaclasses and class creation, SOLID principles applied to real Python code, and the classic comparisons (class method vs static method, __new__ vs __init__, abstract base class vs duck typing). Every answer comes with a short code snippet, the gotcha the interviewer is listening for, and the follow-up they'll ask if you get the first part right.

modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithms in Python
modules.intro: Data structures and algorithms interview questions in Python test both your CS fundamentals and your knowledge of the standard library. This page covers Big-O for Python's built-in operations (list append vs insert, dict lookup, set membership), sorting with key functions and the Timsort guarantee, binary search with bisect, heapq for priority queues, collections.deque for O(1) pops from both ends, and the algorithmic patterns interviewers pair with Python roles: two pointers, sliding window, BFS/DFS with a stack or deque, and basic dynamic programming. For asyncio data structures (asyncio.Queue, asyncio.PriorityQueue) see the Concurrency & Async page.

modules.title: Generators, Decorators & Functional Python
modules.intro: Generators, decorators, and closures are where Python interviews separate candidates who learned syntax from candidates who learned the language. This page covers the iterator protocol (__iter__ and __next__), generator functions with yield, generator expressions, send() and throw() for two-way coroutines, the @decorator pattern and @functools.wraps, LEGB scope resolution, the late-binding closure gotcha, and the context-manager protocol via __enter__/__exit__ and @contextmanager. Every concept is anchored to a real production use case — rate-limit decorators, connection-manager context managers, lazy CSV readers as generators — not toy examples.

modules.title: Concurrency: Threads, Processes & asyncio
modules.intro: Python concurrency interview questions are the most misunderstood topic in the language. This page untangles the three models — threading (I/O-bound, blocked by the GIL), multiprocessing (CPU-bound, separate interpreter per process), and asyncio (I/O-bound, single-threaded cooperative multitasking) — and tells you clearly when each one wins. It covers the GIL in depth (what it protects, when it's released, what Python 3.13's free-threaded mode changes), async/await coroutines, asyncio.gather vs asyncio.create_task, how to avoid blocking the event loop, and the concurrent.futures abstraction over both threads and processes. The scenario questions are the ones companies actually ask: 'our endpoint is slow — is it CPU or I/O?' and 'why did our thread pool make things worse?'

modules.title: CPython Internals & Performance
modules.intro: CPython internals questions test whether you understand what's actually happening when your Python code runs. This page covers reference counting as the primary memory-management strategy, cyclic garbage collection for reference cycles, the three GC generations and when to call gc.collect(), the bytecode layer (dis module, .pyc files, the code object), small integer caching and string interning, and profiling Python applications with cProfile, line_profiler, and memory_profiler. These questions come up more than most candidates expect — especially at companies running Python at scale where a memory leak or a slow hot path costs real money.

modules.title: Django Core
modules.intro: Django interview questions are the backbone of any Python backend screen. This page covers the MTV architecture (how it maps to MVC), the complete request lifecycle from URLconf to middleware to view to template rendering, Django middleware (what it is, how to write it, execution order), class-based views vs function-based views, Django's authentication and permission system, the admin site, and the comparisons that always come up (Django vs Flask vs FastAPI, CBV vs FBV, @login_required vs LoginRequiredMixin). Every answer traces the order-of-events the way a senior Django developer would, not the way the docs read top-to-bottom.

modules.title: Django REST Framework (DRF)
modules.intro: Django REST Framework interview questions go deep on the abstractions that make DRF both powerful and occasionally confusing. This page covers serializers (ModelSerializer vs Serializer, validation hooks, nested serializers, performance), ViewSets and Routers (the naming convention, the trade-off vs APIView), DRF's permission classes and authentication backends (SessionAuthentication, TokenAuthentication, JWT with SimpleJWT), filtering and pagination (DjangoFilterBackend, CursorPagination vs PageNumberPagination), and the scenario questions that come up in real interviews: 'your DRF endpoint is slow — where do you look first?' and 'how would you version this API?'

modules.title: FastAPI
modules.intro: FastAPI interview questions cover the framework that's become the default choice for new Python API projects. This page covers the path-operation function model, Pydantic v2 request/response validation, FastAPI's Depends() dependency injection system (how it composes, how it handles teardown, how to test it), async path operations (when await matters and when it doesn't), background tasks, OpenAPI auto-documentation, and the comparisons that come up in every FastAPI interview: FastAPI vs Django REST Framework vs Flask-RESTful, sync vs async handlers, and Pydantic models vs marshmallow.

modules.title: Flask
modules.intro: Flask interview questions tend to focus on what Flask deliberately leaves out and how you fill those gaps. This page covers Flask's application and request context (the g object, current_app, the why behind the thread-local proxy design), Blueprints for structuring larger applications, Flask-SQLAlchemy and the db.session pattern, Flask-Login for authentication, app factory pattern for testing, and the critical comparisons: Flask vs Django vs FastAPI and when each one is the right choice. If you're interviewing at a startup or a shop that built its API layer on Flask, these questions will come up in the first 20 minutes.

modules.title: SQLAlchemy & Alembic
modules.intro: SQLAlchemy interview questions test both the ORM layer and the core expression language. This page covers the declarative model system, the Session as a unit of work (identity map, expire_on_commit, when to use scoped_session), relationship loading strategies (lazy, eager, selectin, subquery — and when each causes N+1), Alembic migration workflow (autogenerate, upgrade, downgrade, multi-head resolution), the Core layer for raw-SQL-shaped queries with bound parameters, and the scenario questions that distinguish SQLAlchemy power users: 'your query is slow — show me how you'd diagnose it' and 'how do you handle a migration on a table with 100 million rows?'

modules.title: PostgreSQL with Python
modules.intro: PostgreSQL with Python interview questions cover the layer between the ORM and the wire. This page covers psycopg2 (the synchronous default, connection pooling with psycopg2.pool, the cursor types), asyncpg (the async alternative used with FastAPI and asyncio applications, prepared statements, binary protocol), query patterns (parameterised queries, RETURNING clause, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE for upserts), index types in Postgres (B-tree, GIN for JSONB, partial indexes), EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and the production-grade questions: 'your query is doing a sequential scan — walk me through fixing it' and 'how do you handle a long-running migration without locking the table?'

modules.title: MongoDB with Python
modules.intro: MongoDB with Python interview questions cover both PyMongo for sync applications and Motor for async ones. This page covers the document model vs relational model trade-offs, PyMongo's collection API (find, find_one, insert_one, update_one with $set, delete_one, bulk_write for throughput), indexing in MongoDB (single-field, compound, text, TTL), the aggregation pipeline ($match, $group, $lookup, $project, $unwind), Motor for asyncio applications, and the hard questions: 'when would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?' and 'how do you handle schema evolution in a document store when you can't do a migration?'

modules.title: Redis & Caching
modules.intro: Redis interview questions for Python backends cover both the data structures and the patterns built on top of them. This page covers the six core data structures (string, list, hash, set, sorted set, stream), the redis-py client (pipeline for batching, connection pool, Lua scripting), caching patterns (cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind — and when each breaks), TTL and eviction policies (LRU, LFU, volatile-lru), Redis pub/sub vs Kafka for messaging, and the scenario questions: 'cache is returning stale data — how do you diagnose it?' and 'how would you implement a distributed rate limiter using Redis?'

modules.title: REST API Design with Python
modules.intro: REST API design interview questions test whether you've built APIs at scale, not just followed a tutorial. This page covers REST constraints (stateless, uniform interface, resource-based URLs), HTTP verb semantics and idempotency, status code selection (the 200 vs 201 vs 204, 400 vs 401 vs 403 vs 422 debates), API versioning strategies and their trade-offs, cursor-based pagination, JWT authentication with Python (PyJWT, python-jose, SimpleJWT in DRF), rate limiting patterns, and the design questions: 'how would you design the versioning strategy for a public API with 200 API consumers?' and 'why is your POST /payments endpoint causing duplicate charges?'

modules.title: asyncio Deep Dive
modules.intro: asyncio deep-dive interview questions are where Python async separates seniors from juniors. This page goes below the async def surface to cover the event loop's I/O selector, the difference between a coroutine object and a Task, asyncio.gather vs asyncio.create_task vs asyncio.wait, how to bridge sync and async code with loop.run_in_executor, asyncio.Queue for producer-consumer patterns, the common failure modes (blocking call in a coroutine, forgotten await, task exceptions silently swallowed), and the debugging tools (asyncio debug mode, PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG, aiomonitor). These questions come up at companies building high-concurrency Python services — fintech, realtime APIs, ML inference endpoints.

modules.title: WebSockets & Server-Sent Events
modules.intro: WebSocket and SSE interview questions come up whenever a role involves realtime features — chat, dashboards, live notifications. This page covers WebSocket handshake and the full-duplex connection model, the websockets library and FastAPI's WebSocket endpoint, connection lifecycle management (ping/pong, disconnection detection, broadcast patterns), Server-Sent Events as the simpler one-way alternative, the canonical comparison (WebSockets vs SSE vs polling vs long-polling vs MQTT), and how to scale WebSocket connections horizontally using Redis pub/sub as the coordination layer.

modules.title: Celery & Beat
modules.intro: Celery interview questions come up at almost every Python backend company — it's the default tool for background jobs, periodic tasks, and async workflows. This page covers task definition (@shared_task, bind=True, max_retries), broker and result-backend configuration (Redis vs RabbitMQ as broker, Redis vs Django DB as result backend), task routing to named queues, Celery Canvas primitives for complex workflows (chain, group, chord, si() for immutable signatures), Celery Beat for scheduled tasks, monitoring with Flower, and the scenario questions: 'a Celery task is silently failing — how do you find it?' and 'how do you make a Celery task idempotent so retries are safe?'

modules.title: Kafka with Python
modules.intro: Kafka with Python interview questions bridge the core Kafka concepts with Python-specific client behaviour. This page covers the confluent-kafka-python library (producer with delivery callbacks, consumer with manual offset commit), the consumer group rebalance model, offset management strategies (auto-commit vs manual, at-least-once vs exactly-once), error handling in the consumer loop (dead-letter topics, poison-pill messages), schema registry with Avro or JSON Schema, and the scenario questions: 'a consumer is falling behind — how do you diagnose and fix the lag?' and 'how do you safely restart a consumer group after a 6-hour outage without reprocessing everything?'

modules.title: RabbitMQ with Python
modules.intro: RabbitMQ interview questions for Python cover the messaging patterns the AMQP model enables. This page covers the exchange types (direct, topic, fanout, headers), the queue-binding model, durable queues and persistent messages, message acknowledgement (basic_ack, basic_nack, basic_reject), the pika library for Python (blocking vs async connection), dead-letter exchanges for poison messages, and the canonical comparison: RabbitMQ vs Kafka — traditional message queue vs distributed log, when you need each, and the failure modes you're trading into when you pick one over the other.

modules.title: Design Patterns in Python
modules.intro: Design patterns in Python interview questions test whether you know the pattern or just the name. This page covers the GoF patterns as Python expresses them — singleton via module-level state or __new__, factory via class methods or abstract factories, strategy via first-class functions or ABC, observer via callbacks or event emitters, decorator (the Python language feature vs the GoF pattern), and the patterns that are uniquely Pythonic: using generators as coroutines, the descriptor protocol, and context managers as the resource-acquisition pattern. Every answer starts with the decision being made, not the definition: 'when would you reach for strategy over a chain of if/elif blocks?'

modules.title: Clean Architecture & Hexagonal in Python
modules.intro: Clean architecture interview questions in Python come up most at companies that have already outgrown a Django monolith and are thinking about how to restructure. This page covers the classic layered model for Django and FastAPI apps, hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters in Python — how to define a Repository protocol, how to inject the real Postgres adapter vs the in-memory test adapter), CQRS with command and query handlers, event-driven patterns with Django Signals vs domain events, and the practical question every Python architect faces: how much clean architecture is right for a 10k-line codebase vs a 100k-line one?

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.intro: System design fundamentals questions are language-agnostic, but how you answer them is coloured by your stack. This page covers the building blocks every system design answer needs: capacity estimation with real numbers (write rate, read rate, storage, bandwidth), caching strategies and their failure modes (thundering herd, cache stampede, stale reads), load balancing and horizontal scaling, the CAP theorem in practice (which systems are CP, which are AP, and what the P actually means), database sharding strategies, and the trade-off framing that separates good system design answers from great ones. Examples are anchored to Python services — FastAPI behind an ALB, Celery workers scaling on queue depth, Redis as the shared state layer.

modules.title: System Design Case Studies
modules.intro: System design case studies give you the worked examples to anchor abstract concepts. This page walks through five canonical problems with Python-anchored implementations: URL shortener (FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Redis for redirect cache), distributed rate limiter (Redis token bucket, Lua script for atomicity), notification service (Celery + SendGrid + FCM + SQS for fan-out), chat system (WebSockets + Redis pub/sub for horizontal scaling), and social feed (fan-out-on-write for most users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities). Each case study follows the archetype F beat structure: requirements → capacity numbers → API design → data model → high-level architecture → bottleneck deep-dive → trade-offs.

modules.title: Application Security & OWASP in Python
modules.intro: Application security interview questions for Python cover both the theoretical OWASP top 10 and the Python-specific ways each vulnerability manifests. This page covers SQL injection (why parameterised queries with psycopg2/SQLAlchemy are safe, the anti-patterns that aren't), XSS in Django templates (auto-escaping and when it fails), CSRF protection (Django's middleware, FastAPI without sessions), insecure deserialization (why pickle over the network is dangerous), JWT security (algorithm confusion attacks, alg:none, signature verification), OAuth 2.0 in Python (Authlib, python-social-auth), secrets management (environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager with boto3, Python-dotenv for local dev), and bcrypt/argon2 for password hashing.

modules.title: pytest & Testing in Python
modules.intro: pytest interview questions test whether you write tests that actually catch bugs or just tests that pass. This page covers pytest's fixture system (scope, yield for teardown, conftest.py, parametrize for data-driven tests), unittest.mock.patch (patch by usage site not definition site, MagicMock, AsyncMock for async code), integration testing with a real database (pytest-django with transactional tests, Testcontainers for PostgreSQL/Redis), factory_boy for test data, the test pyramid applied to a Python service, and TDD in practice. The scenario questions are the real interview differentiators: 'how do you test a function that calls an external API?' and 'your tests pass locally but fail in CI — how do you debug it?'

modules.title: Type Checking with mypy & Pyright
modules.intro: Type checking interview questions test whether you use type hints as documentation or as a safety net. This page covers PEP 484 type annotation syntax, the typing module (Optional, Union, TypeVar, Generic, Protocol, TypedDict, Literal), mypy's strictness settings and how to introduce it incrementally into an untyped codebase, Pyright vs mypy trade-offs, runtime validation with Pydantic vs static analysis with mypy, and the questions that test real understanding: 'what is a Protocol and how is it different from an ABC?' and 'how do you type a function that can return different types depending on its inputs?'

modules.title: Docker for Python Applications
modules.intro: Docker interview questions for Python applications cover the specifics that make Python containers different from Java or Go ones. This page covers writing an efficient Dockerfile for Python (layer caching strategy — copy requirements first, copy source last), multi-stage builds for smaller production images, the PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE and PYTHONUNBUFFERED environment variables and why they matter, running Python as a non-root user, gunicorn vs uvicorn as the process manager, Docker Compose for local development stacks (FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Redis + Celery worker), health checks, and the scenario questions: 'your Python container is rebuilding from scratch on every push — why?' and 'how do you handle secrets in a Docker container without baking them into the image?'

modules.title: CI/CD for Python Projects
modules.intro: CI/CD for Python interview questions test whether you've actually shipped production Python services or just run tests on your laptop. This page covers a complete GitHub Actions pipeline for Python (lint with ruff/flake8, type-check with mypy, test with pytest + coverage, build and push Docker image, deploy), caching pip and poetry installs for fast CI, running Postgres and Redis as service containers in CI, deployment strategies (blue-green, canary, rolling for a Python web service), Dependabot for dependency security, and the scenario questions that come up in ops-heavy roles: 'your deploy pipeline is taking 12 minutes — show me the first 3 things you'd optimize' and 'a failing test is blocking the release — what do you do?'

modules.title: Python Packaging & Dependency Management
modules.intro: Python packaging interview questions are asked more than most candidates expect, especially at companies that publish internal or external packages. This page covers virtual environments (venv, virtualenv, the why behind isolation), pyproject.toml as the modern project metadata standard, Poetry (dependency groups, lock file, the difference between add and install), pip-compile for deterministic builds, the differences between requirements.txt, setup.py, setup.cfg, and pyproject.toml, publishing to PyPI with twine or poetry publish, and the production questions: 'how do you prevent a transitive dependency upgrade from breaking your service?' and 'your Docker image installs packages at runtime — why is that dangerous?'

modules.title: AWS with Python (boto3)
modules.intro: AWS with Python interview questions cover the boto3 patterns that production teams use every day. This page covers the boto3 client vs resource abstraction, the credential chain (never hardcode keys), S3 operations (upload, download, presigned URLs, multipart for large files), DynamoDB with boto3 (put_item, query, scan, the difference and why scan is expensive), Lambda in Python (cold starts, handler function, context object, best practices for keeping lambdas fast), SQS for decoupled async processing, SNS for fan-out, and IAM roles for service-to-service auth. The scenario questions are the production ones: 'your Lambda is timing out — what are the first three things you check?' and 'how do you safely rotate an IAM access key that's being used by a running service?'

modules.title: Observability & Monitoring for Python
modules.intro: Observability interview questions for Python test whether you can diagnose production problems using evidence, not guessing. This page covers structured logging with structlog or Python's logging module configured for JSON output, correlation IDs propagated via contextvars, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry (instrumenting a FastAPI or Django app, propagating trace context across Celery tasks), Prometheus metrics with prometheus-client (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, the four golden signals), Sentry for error tracking and performance monitoring, and the scenario questions: 'your p99 latency spiked — walk me through the investigation' and 'how do you trace a slow request that touched three Python services and two Celery tasks?'

modules.title: Production Operations & SRE for Python
modules.intro: Production operations interview questions for Python cover the gap between 'it works on my machine' and 'it works at 3am under load'. This page covers SLI/SLO/SLA applied to a Python web service, error budgets and how they drive deployment decisions, the incident response playbook (from on-call page to blameless postmortem), Python-specific performance profiling (cProfile for CPU, memory_profiler and tracemalloc for memory, py-spy for production profiling without code changes), gunicorn/uvicorn worker sizing, Celery worker tuning, and capacity planning questions: 'how do you size the number of gunicorn workers?' and 'how do you find a memory leak in a Python service that's been running for three weeks?'

modules.title: Behavioral & STAR
modules.intro: Behavioral interview questions for Python engineers are the same questions every engineer faces, but the best answers are anchored to real Python projects and real production incidents. This page covers the STAR format with the reflection beat that separates rehearsed answers from self-aware ones, conflict resolution (technical disagreement over Django vs FastAPI, ORM vs raw SQL), failure stories (the production incident you caused, the migration that went wrong), leadership moments (introducing type checking to an untyped codebase, mentoring a junior through their first async bug), and the questions that test engineering values: code review philosophy, technical debt strategy, and how you make architecture decisions under uncertainty.

modules.title: Engineering Practices & Technical Leadership
modules.intro: Engineering practices interview questions are the questions that filter for senior and staff Python engineers. This page covers code review (what to review first, how to give feedback that lands, how to handle a PR you fundamentally disagree with), technical debt strategy (how to make the case for refactoring a 50k-line Django monolith, how to prioritise what to fix first), Architecture Decision Records for Python projects (when to write one, what goes in it, how to get buy-in), and mentoring (how to help a junior engineer through their first asyncio confusion or their first production incident). Every answer uses the reflection beat — not 'here's what I did', but 'here's what I learned and what I'd do differently'.

modules.title: AI & LLM Integration
modules.intro: AI and LLM integration is now a first-class interview topic for Python backend engineers. Hiring loops at product companies ask about calling the OpenAI/Anthropic SDK correctly (sync vs async clients, retry handling, cost estimation), building RAG pipelines with a retriever + generation step, choosing and querying a vector store, structuring LLM outputs with Pydantic, streaming tokens over SSE, designing AI agent loops with tool-calling, and — critically — how you test features whose output is non-deterministic. This module covers the full stack from the API call to the eval harness.
